checks.claim: Key: the mantle makes up about 84 percent of Earth's volume
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'approximately 84% of Earth's total volume and 67% of its mass'; Internal structure page agrees ('roughly 84% of Earth's volume').

checks.claim: 84 percent is far more than the other three layers together (about 16 percent)
checks.note: Core radius about 3,480 km of 6,371 km gives the core about 16 percent of the volume; crust under 1 percent.

checks.claim: Wrong: inner core, outer core, crust (none is the 84 percent layer)
checks.note: Crust 'less than 1% of Earth's total volume'; the inner core (radius about 1,220 km) is under 1 percent; the outer core about 15 percent.

checks.claim: Context: mantle from the crust's base to about 2,900 km, the thickest layer
checks.note: 'The total thickness of the mantle is about 2,900 km'; 'the thickest layer of the planet'. Outer core about 2,260 km, inner core radius about 1,220 km.

checks.claim: Context: the two core layers hold almost all the rest; the crust less than 1 percent
Key: crust usually thinnest under the floor of the open ocean
checks.note: Oceanic crust 'about 5 to 10 kilometers under the oceans'; continental 30 to 50 km, up to 70 km.

checks.claim: Wrong: under a shallow sea near a coast (continental shelf is continental crust, thicker)
checks.note: Shelf is 'the gently sloping, submerged prolongation of a continent's continental crust', 'underlain primarily by continental crust'. Margin profiles (e.g. Grand Banks about 30 km, Morocco 35 km) show the crust thins mainly near the shelf break and beyond; 'usually' in the stem covers rifted exceptions.

checks.claim: Wrong: under high mountains / under the middle of a continent (thick continental crust)
checks.note: 'maximum thicknesses exceeding 70 km beneath major mountain belts'.

checks.claim: Context: oceanic crust usually 5-10 km; continental several times thicker; thickest under high mountains
checks.note: 'Oceanic crust is typically 5 to 10 kilometers'; continental 'averages 30 to 70 kilometers'.

checks.claim: Context: a shallow sea near a coast often covers the drowned edge of a continent, thick continental crust beneath
checks.note: True of the inner shelf (about 30-40 km); crust thins toward the shelf break, but 'often' keeps it safe.

checks.claim: The deepest hole ever drilled (Kola Superdeep Borehole) is still the record by depth
checks.note: Grokipedia: Kola 'maintains the record for the deepest true vertical borehole'. Longer wells (Al Shaheen 12,289 m long) are not deeper; China's Shenditake 1 finished in Feb 2025 at 10,910 m, second in the world (https://globaltimes.cn/page/202502/1328780.shtml). The stem says 'deepest', not 'longest', so it survives; a future well could change it.

checks.claim: Bored into the hard rock of a continent, in the far north of Russia
checks.note: Pechengsky District, Murmansk Oblast, Kola Peninsula near the Norwegian border; Baltic Shield gneiss and granite (continental crust).

checks.claim: Drillers worked at it for about 20 years
checks.note: Began 24 May 1970; record 12,262 m in 1989 (19 years); drilling halted 1992 (Grokipedia) or ended 1995 (Wikipedia). 'About 20 years' is fair.

checks.claim: Got a little more than 12 km down
checks.note: 'maximum true vertical depth of 12,262 metres (40,230 ft) in 1989'.

checks.claim: Key: partway through the crust
checks.note: Crust there 35-40 km (Grokipedia) / about 35 km (Wikipedia); the hole went 'approximately one-third of the continental crust thickness'.

checks.claim: Wrong: just past the crust into the mantle / halfway through the mantle / top of the outer core
checks.note: All far deeper than 12.3 km (Moho about 35 km; outer core about 2,900 km).

checks.claim: Context: crust about 35 km; hole about a third of the way through; about 0.2 percent of the way to the centre
checks.note: 'just 0.2% of the distance to the planet's core' (12.26 / 6,371 = 0.19 percent).

checks.claim: Context: 'No drill has ever reached the mantle, let alone the core.'
checks.note: In 2023 IODP Expedition 399 drilled 1,268 m into mantle rock (serpentinized peridotite) at the Atlantis Massif, where mantle rock lies exposed on the Atlantic seafloor; news reports called it a record hole 'into Earth's mantle' (e.g. https://gizmodo.com/epic-drilling-mission-sets-new-record-with-4160-foot-mantle-core-2000484808). No drill has gone DOWN THROUGH the crust into the mantle, but the bare sentence can be read as false. Fix: 'No drill has ever bored down through the crust into the mantle beneath it, let alone the core.'

checks.claim: Stem: near the core the mantle is more than 3,000 degrees Celsius
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'exceeding 3,000°C near the core boundary'; NatGeo 3,700 °C (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/mantle/); Wikipedia about 4,200 K (3,900 °C) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_mantle).

checks.claim: Key: most of the mantle is solid, yet flows very slowly
checks.note: 'the slow, creeping motion of the Earth's solid silicate mantle'; Wikipedia: 'predominantly solid but, on geologic time scales, it behaves as a viscous fluid'.

checks.claim: Wrong: liquid like lava
checks.note: 'The enormous lithostatic pressure exerted on the mantle prevents melting.'

checks.claim: Wrong: solid and never moves at all
checks.note: It creeps (solid-state flow over geological time).

checks.claim: Wrong: half melted like slushy snow
checks.note: Melt is only about 1-3 percent, and only in a thin layer (lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary). NatGeo calls the asthenosphere 'semi-molten', but the stem asks about MOST of the mantle, which is solid; not defensible.

checks.claim: Context: creeps about 1 to 10 cm a year
checks.note: 'sluggish velocities of 1-10 cm/year'; interior flow 'on the order of ~1 cm/yr', plates 2-5 cm/yr.

checks.claim: Context: only small parts partly melted; not a sea of magma
checks.note: 'containing 1% to 3% melt' at the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary.

checks.claim: Stem: outer core lies below the mantle, more than 2,000 km thick
checks.note: About 2,890 to 5,150 km deep, 'a thickness of about 2,260 kilometers'; NatGeo 'about 2,200 kilometers'.

checks.claim: Key: liquid iron and nickel
checks.note: 'a fluid layer of molten metal', 'primarily composed of iron and nickel'; NatGeo 'mostly composed of liquid iron and nickel' (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/core/).

checks.claim: Wrong: solid iron and nickel (that is the inner core)
checks.note: 'The outer core of Earth is liquid, unlike its inner core, which is solid.'

checks.claim: Wrong: liquid melted rock; hot solid rock
checks.note: It is a metal alloy, not silicate rock: 'molten iron-nickel alloy'.

checks.claim: Context: about 85-90 percent iron, some nickel, a little of a few lighter elements
checks.note: '85-90% iron, 5-10% nickel', plus light elements such as sulfur and oxygen (about 10 percent by mass on the Outer core page).

checks.claim: Context: far too deep to be the source of a volcano's lava
checks.note: Magma forms by partial melting in the upper mantle and crust (Wikipedia Earth's mantle: partial melting at ridges and subduction zones); 'Magma comes from Earth's outer core' is a listed misconception.

checks.claim: Stem: at the surface iron melts at about 1,500 degrees Celsius
checks.note: 1,538 °C at 1 atm.

checks.claim: Stem: the inner core is mostly iron
checks.note: 'iron constituting approximately 85-90% by weight and nickel making up 5-10%'.

checks.claim: Stem: the inner core 'is hotter than 5,000 degrees' (Celsius, the stem's unit)
checks.note: Most current figures clear it: Wikipedia 5,400-5,700 K (5,100-5,400 °C), Anzellini 2013 iron melting 5,957 ± 500 °C; NatGeo 5,200 °C; Grokipedia up to 5,400 °C, centre 5,400-6,000 K (5,130-5,730 °C). But the margin is thin and some published figures fall below it: Grokipedia's own Outer core page gives the inner-core boundary as 'roughly 5,000-6,000 K' (from about 4,730 °C), and a 1993 Nature estimate put it at 4,850 ± 200 K (about 4,580 °C) (https://dx.doi.org/10.1038/363534a0). Fix: 'is more than 4,000 degrees' or 'is about as hot as the surface of the Sun'; the question's point (over three times iron's surface melting point) is unchanged.

checks.claim: Key: the enormous pressure keeps it solid
checks.note: 'The inner core is solid at high temperature because of its high pressure'; NatGeo: the pressure 'prevents the iron from melting'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the nickel mixed with the iron
checks.note: Nickel melts at 1,455 °C, lower than iron; it does not explain solidity.

checks.claim: Wrong: the lack of air or oxygen; the pull of the magnetic field
checks.note: Melting is a physical change needing heat, not air; the field is made by the outer core and does not freeze the inner core.

checks.claim: Context: pressure at the centre is millions of times the air's
checks.note: 'nearly 3.6 million atmospheres'; Grokipedia 330 GPa at the boundary, about 365 GPa at the centre.

checks.claim: Context: under such pressure iron needs far more heat to melt; nickel melts lower than iron
checks.note: 'its melting temperature increases dramatically at pressures of that magnitude'; iron 1,538 °C, nickel 1,455 °C.

checks.claim: Stem: the world's deepest mine reaches about 4 km underground
checks.note: Mponeng, South Africa: 'approximately 4 kilometers', 'the world's deepest underground mine'; Wikipedia 'over 4 kilometres' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mponeng_Gold_Mine). A record that could change, but 'about 4 km' survives small deepening.

checks.claim: Stem: bare rock about 60 degrees Celsius
checks.note: Wikipedia 66 °C; Grokipedia 'exceeding 60°C'.

checks.claim: Stem: ice is pumped down to cool the tunnels
checks.note: 'the mine pumps slurry ice underground to cool the tunnel air to below 30 °C'.

checks.claim: Key: heat flows up from deep inside Earth
checks.note: Heat flows outward by conduction from the hotter interior; gradient about 25-30 °C per km in typical continental crust.

checks.claim: Wrong: the Sun's heat soaks down
checks.note: Solar/seasonal effects only in the upper 10-30 m.

checks.claim: Wrong: melted rock just beneath the mine; hot water seeping down from the surface
checks.note: Witwatersrand Basin is old stable continental crust with no magma; surface water is cooler, not hotter.

checks.claim: Context: the Sun's warmth reaches only the top 20 metres or so
checks.note: Seasonal variation fades within about 8-20 m (Wikipedia); Grokipedia says solar/seasonal effects in the upper 10-30 m. 'About 20 metres or so' fits both.

checks.claim: Context: no melted rock under the mine
Key: the inner core is the hotter layer
checks.note: Outer core 'roughly 4,000 K near the core-mantle boundary to 5,700 K at its inner boundary'; inner core 'around 5,700-6,000 K at the inner core boundary'; EBSCO: 'Temperature increases with distance from the surface', about 6,100 °C at the centre (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/earth-and-atmospheric-sciences/earths-core).

checks.claim: Wrong: the outer core is hotter / the two equally hot
checks.note: The outer core runs from about 3,000-4,500 K at its top up to the boundary value; the inner core is at or above the boundary value throughout. NatGeo's figures (inner 5,200 °C inside an outer-core range of 4,500-5,500 °C, and the boundary called the hottest part) are muddled, but the physics and Grokipedia/Wikipedia/EBSCO make the inner core hotter. Not defensible.

checks.claim: Wrong: both cooler than the mantle
checks.note: Mantle runs about 230 °C at the top to about 3,900 °C at the core boundary; both core layers are hotter.

checks.claim: Context: temperature keeps rising toward the centre; inner core hottest layer, about as hot as the Sun's surface
checks.note: 'approximately 5,700 K (5,430 °C)', 'about the temperature at the surface of the Sun' (photosphere about 5,772 K).

checks.claim: Context: the mantle above both is far cooler
checks.note: Mantle 1,000-3,700 °C (NatGeo). At the core-mantle boundary the two meet at about the same temperature, but as a layer the mantle is far cooler than either core layer; acceptable.

checks.claim: Key: pressure rises because of the weight of all the rock above
checks.note: Overburden pressure is from 'the weight of the overlying rock, soil, sediment, and pore fluids'; it 'increases with depth', about 1 psi/ft (22.7 kPa/m).

checks.claim: Wrong: heat from the core pushing outward
checks.note: Pressure at depth is from gravity on the overlying load, not heat.

checks.claim: Wrong: Earth's spin squeezing it inward
checks.note: Rotation lets material 'flow outward, forming the bulge'; about 21.4 km between equatorial and polar radii.

checks.claim: Wrong: the pull of the Moon from above
checks.note: Tides are tiny and pull outward, not a squeeze that grows with depth.

checks.claim: Context: only 5 km down the pressure is more than a thousand times the air's
checks.note: At about 5 km 'approximately 130-140 MPa (roughly 1,300-1,400 atmospheres)'; 22.7 MPa/km x 5 km = 113 MPa, about 1,100 atm, still over a thousand.

checks.claim: Context: spin makes Earth bulge outward at the equator
checks.note: 'The primary cause of the equatorial bulge is the planet's rotation.'

checks.claim: Stem: young Earth largely melted; much of its iron gathered at the centre as the core
checks.note: Magma oceans about 4.5 billion years ago from giant impacts; core formation complete within about 30 million years.

checks.claim: Key: iron is denser than rock, so it sank
checks.note: 'heavier elements like iron sinking toward the center while lighter silicates rise to the surface', driven by density differences; NatGeo: 'Droplets of iron, nickel, and other heavy metals gravitated to the center' (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/core/).

checks.claim: Wrong: iron is magnetic, so it was pulled inward
checks.note: The page treats magnetism as a consequence of a liquid core, not a driver; hot iron above about 770 °C (its Curie point) is not magnetic anyway.

checks.claim: Wrong: the Sun's heat drove it inward; iron cooled first and hardened in the middle
checks.note: Neither is the mechanism; the core formed as liquid metal sinking, and the outer core is still liquid.

checks.claim: Context: layers sorted by density, dense metal core at centre, light crust on top
checks.note: Core about 11 g/cm3, mantle about 4.4, crust about 2.7.

unit_notes: Two uncertain, both one-line fixes; every key is sound. (1) ea1da3c355 context: 'No drill has ever reached the mantle' clashes with the 2023 Atlantis Massif hole (1,268 m into mantle rock exposed on the Atlantic seafloor); say 'bored down through the crust into the mantle beneath it'. (2) 481c691281 stem: 'hotter than 5,000 degrees' holds for current mainstream figures (about 5,100-6,000 C) but the margin is thin and some published values for the inner core's edge fall below 5,000 C; 'more than 4,000 degrees' or 'about as hot as the surface of the Sun' is safe. Records checked Nov 2026: Kola (12,262 m) is still the deepest vertical hole (Shenditake 1 stopped at 10,910 m in Feb 2025); Mponeng is still the deepest mine (about 4 km).
